content: A refreshable Braille display, also known as a Braille terminal, is an electro-mechanical device designed to present Braille characters. It achieves this by raising dots through small holes on a flat surface. This device is primarily used by blind individuals who are unable to utilize a standard computer monitor, allowing them to read text output. In addition to refreshable Braille displays, speech synthesizers are also commonly employed for the same purpose. Depending on the situation, a blind user may alternate between these two systems or use them simultaneously. Due to the intricate engineering required to create a durable and reliable display capable of withstanding daily use, these devices are typically expensive. Most refreshable Braille displays feature either 40 or 80 Braille cells, though some notetaker devices are equipped with models that have between 18 and 40 cells. Certain models incorporate features such as vibrating dots to indicate the cursor's position, while others include a switch for each cell, enabling the user to move the cursor directly to a specific cell. The mechanism responsible for raising the Braille dots relies on the piezoelectric effect, a property of certain crystals that expand when an electrical voltage is applied. Each dot in the display is connected to a crystal, which, when activated, moves a lever to raise the dot. Since each Braille character consists of eight dots, eight crystals are required per character. The software that operates the refreshable Braille display is referred to as a screen reader. This software extracts the content displayed on the screen from the operating system, translates it into Braille characters, and transmits it to the display. Screen readers designed for graphical operating systems are particularly complex, as they must interpret and convert visual elements such as windows and sliders into text descriptions. Modern operating systems often provide an Application Programming Interface (API) to facilitate this process. For example, Microsoft Windows uses Microsoft Active Accessibility (MSAA), while GNOME employs Assistive Technology Service Provider Interface (AT-SPI). A novel innovation in this field, known as the rotating-wheel Braille display, was introduced in 2000 by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). A second version of this technology was later developed by Leuven University in Belgium. However, both designs are still undergoing commercialization. In this system, Braille dots are positioned along the edge of a rotating wheel. The user can read continuously by keeping their finger stationary while the wheel spins at a chosen speed. The Braille dots are set in place as the wheel rotates past a fixed actuator that configures the Braille characters. This design significantly reduces manufacturing complexity, making rotating-wheel Braille displays more affordable than traditional models. Historically, the foundation of the refreshable Braille display lies in the concept of a pure Braille terminal. These devices allowed input through two sets of three keys and a space bar, similar to the Perkins Brailler, while output was provided via a refreshable Braille display composed of electromechanical character cells. Each cell could raise or lower a combination of six round-tipped pins to form Braille characters. Variants of this design include devices that use a standard QWERTY keyboard for input and Braille pins for output, as well as devices that are exclusively input-only or output-only. In 1951, David Abraham, a woodworking instructor at the Perkins School for the Blind, developed a portable Braille terminal, marking a significant milestone in the history of Braille technology.
